messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely means the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? Actually, they might want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That would be sigma/sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; we have sample std dev 1.4. Usually use sample std dev as estimate of sigma. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. So answer ~0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic is sqrt((n-1)/n)? Actually t-statistic has distribution with df=39, but its standard deviation is sqrt(df/(df-2)) if df>2. For df=39, sqrt(39/37)=sqrt(1.05405)=1.0268. But that's not what they ask. They ask "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test". Might be the standard error of the mean under null. So answer ~0.2215.

Thus respond with that.
